newsitem.title: MALTA: Malta on countdown towards Europe or neutrality.
newsitem.headline: Malta on countdown towards Europe or neutrality.

text.p: Election officials on Sunday laboriously counted votes under watchful eyes after a record turnout in Malta's general election, which will decide whether the Mediterranean island joins the European Union.
At stake is the future of Malta's application to join the EU, to be pursued if the former ruling Nationalist Party wins and scrapped if the opposition Labour Party achieves victory.
Prime Minister Edward Fenech Adami, 62, who had a three-seat majority in the 65-member parliament, is pledged to pursue the EU membership application he made in 1990.
Labour leader Alfred Sant, 48, is committed to end Malta's application and pull the country from NATO's Partnership for Peace Programme which it joined last year.
Malta has no independent opinion polls and both main parties say their own polls show they will win.
Results were not expected until late on Sunday or early on Monday, despite efforts to speed up counting after repeated complaints.
Delegates from the main parties and the small Democratic Alternative, behind a perspex "cage" enclosing the counting area, scrutinised each vote with its long list of candidates.
Violent hammering on the perspex and a clamour over the validity of a vote often disrupted proceedings, once for over 15 minutes as a Democratic Alternative militant argued vehemently.
Turnout from Saturday's poll was a record 97 percent of the nearly 275,000 electorate.
Votes for Sant and for Fenech Adami built in steady piles in the red and blue pigeonholes of the parties.

Chief electoral commissioner Carmell Portelli, giving the turnout figure at a news conference at the counting hall near the ancient walled Arab city of Mdina, said: "So far, this election has been plain sailing."
Malta's Sunday Times said the turnout and incident-free vote "shows that voters could make their all-important choice responsibly, without fear or favour".
Elections in the 1970s and 1980s were marked by violence which both parties pledged to avoid, the Labour Party banning its supporters from putting up banners to avoid strife.
Reflecting the intimate nature of the island, election manifestos ranged from international to very local issues.
But with normally only about 5,000 votes between the parties and where turnout usually tops 90 percent, the focus was Europe and its impact on the economy.
Fenech Adami told Reuters on the eve of voting: "I already have a mandate...(but) it will be a sort of another referendum on Malta's membership of the EU."

Sant says membership does not suit the small island and Value Added Tax (VAT) at 15 percent standard, pushed up living costs, brought hardship to ordinary people, and was imposed purely to please Europe. "No other country imposed VAT even before serious negotiations on entry," he said.
For Fenech Adami, Europe "is the only way Malta can go, in our own best interests". He sees EU talks completed and Malta ready for membership by mid-1998.
Labour seeks instead a "special relationship" and what it terms "positive neutrality" as best suited to the island where sovereignty is a sensitive issue.
The Nationalists believe membership will bring reassurance to Malta, sited in an area Fenech Adami calls "turbulent".

Labour, already alarmed at increased visits by Western naval vessels, fears Malta -- awarded the British George Cross in 1942 for its bravery withstanding Italian and German wartime attacks -- being turned back to a fortress island.
Sant said that pulling out of NATO's Partnership for Peace Programme "will be my first priority".
It would be followed by legislation to abolish VAT and replace it with customs tariffs, undercutting a basis of EU membership and signalling Malta's withdrawal of its bid. 271307 GMT oct 96
